  Heuristic search has been very successful in abstract game                  and/or memory requirements. Therefore, it can be challeng-
  domains such as Chess and Go. In video games, however,                      ing to adapt established search algorithms to large scale real-
  adoption has been slow due to the fact that state and move                  time decision problems, e.g. video games and robotics. In
  spaces are much larger, real-time constraints are harsher, and              what follows, we will see how the Alpha-Beta search al-
  constraints on computational resources are tighter. In this pa-             gorithm can be used to solve adversarial real-time planning
  per we present a fast search method — Alpha-Beta search for                 problems with durative moves. We begin by motivating the
  durative moves — that can defeat commonly used AI scripts                   application area — small scale combat in RTS games —
  in RTS game combat scenarios of up to 8 vs. 8 units running                 and discussing relevant literature. We then define our search
  on a single core in under 5ms per search episode. This per-                 problem formally, describe several solution concepts, and
  formance is achieved by using standard search enhancements

  such as transposition tables and iterative deepening, and novel
  usage of combat AI scripts for sorting moves and state evalu-               Durations) which we will evaluate experimentally. We con-
  ation via playouts. We also present evidence that commonly                  clude by discussing future research directions in this area.

               a1             a2                 b1             b2                 game with simultaneous moves, as ROCK - PAPER - SCISSORS
                                                                                   proves. Less intuitively so, the need for randomized strate-
          b1        b2   b1        b2      a1         a2   a1        a2            gies also arises in combat games, even in cases with 2
                                                                                   vs. 2 immobile units (Furtak and Buro (2010)). To mit-
                                                                                   igate the potential unfairness caused by the Minmax and
                                                                                   Maxmin game transformations, (Kovarsky and Buro 2005)
                                                                                   propose the Random-Alpha-Beta (RAB) algorithm. RAB is
                                                                                   a Monte Carlo algorithm that repeatedly performs Alpha-
                Maxmin                            Minmax                           Beta searches in transformed games where the player-to-
                                                                                   move order is randomized in interior simultaneous move
                                        a1 b1                        a2 b2         nodes. Once time runs out, the move with the highest to-
               b1
                                                                                   tal score at the root is chosen. (Kovarsky and Buro 2005)
                                                a1 b2       a2 b1                  shows that RAB can outperform Alpha-Beta search on the
          a1        a2
                                                                                   Maxmin-transformed tree, using iterative deepening and a
                                                                                   simple heuristic evaluation function. In our experiments,
                                                                                   we will test the stripped down RAB version we call RAB’,
                                                                                   which only runs Alpha-Beta once.
